approachQuestion.prompt:
Find an earlier pair for a target

Input: an integer array values and an integer target. Output: the indices [i, j] of any two distinct positions whose values sum to target, or [-1, -1] if no such pair exists. Example 1: values = [4, 9, 1, 6, 5], target = 10 → [1, 2] is valid. Example 2: values = [6], target = 12 → [-1, -1]; one position cannot be used twice. Example 3: values = [3, 3], target = 6 → [0, 1].
constraints: −1,000,000,000 ≤ values[i], target ≤ 1,000,000,000; sums are evaluated in signed 64-bit arithmetic.
Do not mutate the input. Any valid pair is accepted; the two indices must be distinct. If no pair exists, return [-1, -1].
Assume integer-key hash table lookups and insertions have expected amortized constant cost under an ordinary non-adversarial distribution; this is not a worst-case guarantee.

options.text: Scan from left to right. Before storing the current value, look up target − currentValue in a map of earlier values to one earlier index. If found, return those two indices; otherwise store the current value if it is not already present.
options.feedback: The map represents only positions already passed, so a match always uses two distinct indices. Keeping one earlier index per value is sufficient because any valid pair is accepted.

options.text: Sort a copy of (value, originalIndex) pairs, use two pointers to find two values with the target sum, then return their original indices.
options.feedback: This remains correct because the copy preserves each original index and the two pointers use distinct entries. Sorting is removable: a direct complement lookup avoids ordering all entries first.

options.text: Try every pair of distinct indices and return as soon as their values sum to the target.
options.feedback: This is correct but brute force: it repeats pair comparisons even though prior values can be queried directly.

options.text: Store the current value in the map, then look up its complement and return the two associated indices.
options.feedback: The current element can match itself. For values = [6] and target = 12, this returns the same index twice although no valid pair exists.

feedback.reason: Use prior state carefully: the current position must not be eligible as its own partner.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Look up a complement among earlier values” shown after your first answer, choose its expected running time and auxiliary-space pair under this explicit model: For this question, assume integer-key hash operations take expected amortized O(1) time under a non-adversarial hash distribution. State expected time on that basis; do not interpret it as an unconditional worst-case guarantee. Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input arrays and the returned scalar/pair, but includes every map/set and temporary structure.
constraints: For this question, assume integer-key hash operations take expected amortized O(1) time under a non-adversarial hash distribution. State expected time on that basis; do not interpret it as an unconditional worst-case guarantee. Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input arrays and the returned scalar/pair, but includes every map/set and temporary structure.

options.text: Expected O(n) time; O(u) auxiliary space, where u is the number of distinct values stored.
Guaranteed worst-case O(n) time for every hash distribution; O(u) auxiliary space.
O(n log n) time; O(n) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Each input position causes one complement lookup and at most one insertion. The selected pair is assessed under the stated expected/amortized hash model; it is not a deterministic worst-case bound.

details.analyzedMethod: The fixed target uses a map from each previously seen value to one original index. It checks before inserting the current value, so every returned pair uses distinct positions.
details.time: Expected O(n): n expected-constant-time lookups and at most n expected-constant-time insertions. With adversarial collisions, ordinary hash maps can take O(n²) total; no unconditional worst-case O(n) claim is made.
details.additionalSpace: O(u), at most O(n), for saved distinct values and their indices. Input and returned pair are excluded.

q1Alternatives.prior-value-index-map: Correct and the fixed target. It preserves index provenance and checks only earlier positions.
q1Alternatives.sort-value-index-copy: Correct for any valid pair. It sorts a copy of n value/index pairs, then scans them; expected or deterministic comparison sorting takes O(n log n) time and O(n) copy space.
q1Alternatives.enumerate-all-pairs: Correct but brute force, with O(n²) pair checks and O(1) additional space.
q1Alternatives.store-before-lookup: Incorrect: [6], target 12 can reuse the same position.

q2Options.linear-expected-linear-space: Correct under the prompt’s explicit expected/amortized hash-operation assumption.
q2Options.linear-worst-linear-space: Incorrect because the prompt does not guarantee constant-time hash operations under every collision pattern.
q2Options.quadratic-constant-space: Incorrect for the fixed map method: this is looser time than its expected bound.
q2Options.n-log-n-linear-space: Incorrect for the fixed map method: it does not sort.

methodReveal.title: Look up a complement among earlier values
methodReveal.description: Visit values in input order. For the current value, compute target minus that value and check the map containing only earlier values. If the complement is present, return its saved index and the current index. Otherwise, save the current value and its index if this value has not been saved before. If the scan ends, return [-1, -1].
